layoutNote.llama: The Hugging Face names assume the standard LlamaForCausalLM conversion (model.layers.N.…). A file converted from another source layout, such as Mistral's consolidated format or a vision model's language tower, has other source tensor names.
layoutNote.olmoe: The graph is llama.cpp's OLMoE graph. The Hugging Face names are the ones transformers uses in memory (model.layers.N.…): the checkpoint on disk stores the experts one by one (mlp.experts.N.gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj), and transformers stacks them when it loads. Expert routing measurements come from the PyTorch checkpoint run, not from this GGUF.
layoutNote.qwen35moe: The Hugging Face names assume a checkpoint that stores each block's experts fused (model.language_model.layers.N.mlp.experts.gate_up_proj and …down_proj), as the catalog's checkpoints do. A per-expert checkpoint stacks mlp.experts.N.* tensors instead, and no metadata in the file tells which layout it was converted from.

rope.detail: Applied to the queries and keys, not to values; no stored weight of its own. Files converted with Llama 3's RoPE scaling also hold `rope_freqs`: one frequency factor per rotated pair, which slows the slowest pairs further so positions stay distinguishable over a longer context. The other parameters come from the file's metadata.
rope.math:
$$\begin{pmatrix} u'_{2i} \\ u'_{2i+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos p\theta_i & -\sin p\theta_i \\ \sin p\theta_i & \cos p\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_{2i} \\ u_{2i+1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \theta_i = \frac{b^{-i/r}}{f_i}$$

- $u$: one query or key head; $i < r$: llama.cpp pairs neighbouring dimensions.
- $2r$: number of rotated dimensions; the rest pass unchanged.
- $b$: base frequency; $p$: position.
- $f_i$: frequency factor from `rope_freqs` when the file has it, else 1.

Hugging Face's Llama pairs dimension $i$ with $i + r$ instead, so the converter reorders the rows of Q and K to match; the attention scores stay the same.

attn.detail: Keys and values of all earlier tokens and the current one come from the KV cache. Queries and keys arrive normed over the whole projection and rotated by RoPE. llama.cpp's OLMoE graph fixes the scale at $1/\sqrt{d_h}$ and stores no attention weights. A PyTorch trace of the checkpoint can record selected attention rows when "Record attention" is on; the stepper shows them.
attn.math:
$$a^{(j)}_t = \sum_{s \le t} \mathrm{softmax}_s\!\left(\frac{\tilde q^{(j)}_t \cdot \tilde k^{(m)}_s}{\sqrt{d_h}}\right) v^{(m)}_s$$

- $t$: current position; $s$: cached positions.
- $m$: key/value head used by query head $j$.
- $\tilde q$, $\tilde k$: after the whole-projection norm and RoPE.
- $1/\sqrt{d_h}$: the graph fixes it.
attn.overview: Each query head scores the cached keys of its key/value head; the scores become weights that sum to 1, and the output is the weighted mix of the values.

exp_down.detail: `ffn_down_exps` stacks one down matrix per expert; only the chosen experts' matrices are used, and the router weights follow. The checkpoint on disk stores each expert's `mlp.experts.N.down_proj` on its own; `mlp.experts.down_proj` is transformers' stacked tensor in memory.
exp_down.math:
$$E_e(x') = W_{d,e}\,m_e, \qquad e \in S$$

- $m_e$: expert $e$'s SiLU product.
- $W_{d,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_down_exps`, from $d_{\text{exp}}$ to $d$.
exp_down.overview: Maps each chosen expert's wide vector back to the residual width with its slice of `ffn_down_exps`.

exp_gate.detail: `ffn_gate_exps` stacks one gate matrix per expert, stored apart from `ffn_up_exps`; only the chosen experts' matrices are used for this token. The checkpoint on disk stores each expert's `mlp.experts.N.gate_proj` on its own; `mlp.experts.gate_up_proj`, whose first half is the gate, is transformers' fused tensor in memory.
exp_gate.math:
$$g_e = W_{g,e}\,x', \qquad e \in S$$

- $x'$: output of `ffn_norm`, the same for every chosen expert.
- $W_{g,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_gate_exps`, from $d$ to the expert width $d_{\text{exp}}$.
exp_gate.overview: Each chosen expert widens the normed vector into its gate branch with its own slice of `ffn_gate_exps`.

exp_up.detail: `ffn_up_exps` stacks one up matrix per expert, stored apart from `ffn_gate_exps`; only the chosen experts' matrices are used, on the same input as the gate. The checkpoint on disk stores each expert's `mlp.experts.N.up_proj` on its own; in memory transformers holds it as the second half of `mlp.experts.gate_up_proj`.
exp_up.math:
$$u_e = W_{u,e}\,x', \qquad e \in S$$

- $W_{u,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_up_exps`, from $d$ to $d_{\text{exp}}$.
- $x'$: output of `ffn_norm`.
exp_up.overview: Each chosen expert widens the normed vector into its up branch with its own slice of `ffn_up_exps`.

ffn_residual.detail: The unnormed sum from the first residual add plus the routed experts' weighted sum; there is no dense `ffn_down` and no shared expert. This is the block output unless a control vector is loaded.
ffn_residual.math:
$$h'' = h' + y_{\text{routed}}$$

- $h'$: output of the first residual add.
- $y_{\text{routed}}$: the weighted expert sum.
ffn_residual.overview: Adds the weighted sum of the chosen experts to the stream.

k.math:
$$k = W_K\,x + b_K$$

- $W_K$: `attn_k`, or the K rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_{kv} d_h$.
- $b_K$: `attn_k.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the K entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_k.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise (the OLMoE checkpoint has none).
- $n_{kv}$: number of key/value heads.

k_norm.detail: RMSNorm over the whole key projection with `attn_k_norm`: one weight per dimension of the projection, stored as the Hugging Face value. The split into heads and RoPE follow.
k_norm.math:
$$\tilde k = \frac{k}{\mathrm{rms}(k)} \odot w_k$$

- $k$: the whole key projection, length $n_{kv} d_h$.
- $w_k$: `attn_k_norm`, same length.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
k_norm.overview: Normalizes the whole key projection, all key/value heads together, before it is split into heads.

q.math:
$$q = W_Q\,x + b_Q$$

- $W_Q$: `attn_q`, or the Q rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_h d_h$.
- $b_Q$: `attn_q.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the Q entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_q.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise (the OLMoE checkpoint has none).
- $n_h$: number of query heads; $d_h$: head size.

q_norm.detail: RMSNorm over the whole query projection with `attn_q_norm`: one weight per dimension of the projection, stored as the Hugging Face value. The split into heads and RoPE follow.
q_norm.math:
$$\tilde q = \frac{q}{\mathrm{rms}(q)} \odot w_q$$

- $q$: the whole query projection, length $n_h d_h$.
- $w_q$: `attn_q_norm`, same length.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
q_norm.overview: Normalizes the whole query projection, all heads together, before it is split into heads.

rope.detail: Here the normed Q and K become heads of size $d_h$. RoPE then rotates every dimension of each head, pairing each one with the dimension half a head away (llama.cpp's NEOX type). Values are not rotated, and there is no stored weight. The base frequency and any context scaling come from the file's metadata.
rope.math:
$$\begin{pmatrix} u'_i \\ u'_{i+r} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos p\theta_i & -\sin p\theta_i \\ \sin p\theta_i & \cos p\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_i \\ u_{i+r} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \theta_i = b^{-i/r}$$

- $u$: one query or key head; $i < r = d_h/2$, so every dimension rotates.
- $b$: base frequency; $p$: position.
rope.overview: Splits the normed queries and keys into heads, then encodes each token's position by rotating pairs of values within each head.

topk_weights.detail: llama.cpp's OLMoE graph keeps the chosen probabilities as they are (`norm_w = false`), so the weights add up to at most 1. No extra scale is applied: llama.cpp's OLMoE loader never reads `expert_weights_scale`.
topk_weights.math:
$$w_e = p_e, \qquad e \in S, \qquad \sum_{e \in S} w_e \le 1$$

- $p_e$: router probability of expert $e$; $S$: the $k$ chosen experts.
- No division by $\sum_{j \in S} p_j$ and no further scale.
topk_weights.overview: Uses the chosen experts' router probabilities as their weights, without renormalizing them.

v.math:
$$v = W_V\,x + b_V$$

- $W_V$: `attn_v`, or the V rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_{kv} d_h$.
- $b_V$: `attn_v.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the V entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_v.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise (the OLMoE checkpoint has none).

attn.math:
$$a^{(j)}_t = \sum_{s \le t} \mathrm{softmax}_s\!\left(\frac{\tilde q^{(j)}_t \cdot \tilde k^{(m)}_s}{\sqrt{d_h}}\right) v^{(m)}_s$$

- $t$: current position; $s$: cached positions.
- $m$: key/value head shared by query head $j$.
- $\tilde q$, $\tilde k$: queries and keys after norm and RoPE.
- $1/\sqrt{d_h}$: default scale; a file can set another.

attn_norm.detail: RMSNorm with the stored weight `attn_norm`, one value per dimension. Only the mixer sees the normed vector; the residual add uses the unnormed input. In the MTP block the input is the `nextn.eh_proj` output.
attn_norm.math:
$$x = \frac{h}{\mathrm{rms}(h)} \odot w$$

- $h$: block input.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
- $w$: `attn_norm`, stored as $1 + w_{\text{HF}}$.

attn_residual.detail: The unnormed block input plus the mixer's output projection. The sum feeds `post_attention_norm` and is kept for the second residual add.

k.detail: `attn_k` (or the K rows of a fused `attn_qkv`) produces one key per key/value head. There can be fewer key/value heads than query heads (grouped-query attention); each serves a group of query heads. Keys go into the KV cache after norm and RoPE.

mixer_out.detail: `attn_output` takes the concatenated, gated heads and mixes them into one vector of width `n_embd`.
mixer_out.math:
$$y = W_O\,[\,\bar a^{(1)};\dots;\bar a^{(n_h)}\,]$$

- $\bar a^{(j)}$: gated output of query head $j$.
- $W_O$: `attn_output`, from $n_h d_h$ to $d$.
mixer_out.overview: Maps the gated attention output of all heads back to the residual width.

post_norm.detail: RMSNorm with `post_attention_norm`, stored as 1 plus the Hugging Face value. Despite the name it is a pre-norm for the FFN: the residual add uses the unnormed sum.
post_norm.math:
$$x' = \frac{h'}{\mathrm{rms}(h')} \odot w$$

- $h'$: output of the first residual add.
- $w$: `post_attention_norm`.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.

q.detail: `attn_q` (or the Q rows of a fused `attn_qkv`) outputs twice the usual query size: per head, the first half is the query and the second half the gate input.
q.math:
$$[\,q^{(j)}\,;\,g^{(j)}\,] = (W_Q\,x + b_Q)^{(j)}$$

- $W_Q$: `attn_q`, or the Q rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $2 n_h d_h$.
- $b_Q$: `attn_q.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the Q entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_q.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise.
- $j$: query head; $n_h$ heads of size $d_h$.
- $q^{(j)}$: query; $g^{(j)}$: gate input.
q.overview: Projects the normed input into queries, plus a second half per head that becomes the output gate.

rope.detail: Applied to the normed queries and keys, not to values; no stored weight. qwen35 uses multi-axis RoPE (MRoPE): each rotated pair is assigned to a time, height or width position. For text all three positions are equal, so it acts like ordinary RoPE. The parameters come from the file's metadata.
rope.math:
$$\begin{pmatrix} u'_i \\ u'_{i+r} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos p\theta_i & -\sin p\theta_i \\ \sin p\theta_i & \cos p\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_i \\ u_{i+r} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \theta_i = b^{-i/r}$$

- $u$: one query or key head; $i < r$.
- $2r$: number of rotated dimensions; the rest pass unchanged.
- $b$: base frequency; $p$: position.

The score $\langle R_p q, R_s k \rangle$ then depends on $p$ and $s$ only through $p - s$.

ffn_residual.detail: The unnormed sum from the first residual add plus `moe_out`, the routed and shared experts together; this block has no dense `ffn_down`. In a trunk block this is the block output unless a control vector is loaded; in the MTP block it goes to the head norm.
ffn_residual.math:
$$h'' = h' + y$$

- $h'$: output of the first residual add.
- $y$: output of `moe_out`.
ffn_residual.overview: Adds the mixture-of-experts result to the stream.

topk_weights.detail: qwen35moe always renormalizes: the chosen experts' probabilities are divided by their sum, so their weights add up to 1 however much probability the other experts had. No further scale is applied to the weights.
topk_weights.math:
$$w_e = \frac{p_e}{\max\big(\sum_{j \in S} p_j,\ \epsilon\big)}, \qquad e \in S, \qquad \sum_{e \in S} w_e = 1$$

- $p_e$: router probability of expert $e$; $S$: the $k$ chosen experts.
- $\epsilon$: a tiny lower bound llama.cpp puts on the sum, so it never divides by zero.
- llama.cpp's optional extra scale of the weights is unset for qwen35moe, so none applies.
topk_weights.overview: Renormalizes the chosen experts' probabilities so their weights add up to 1.

fullAttention.detail: Input and output are the residual stream: one vector per token, width `n_embd`. A norm prepares the input, attention reads earlier tokens through the KV cache, and the result is added back. A second norm and the feed-forward network follow, again added back.
fullAttention.math:
In the common pre-norm layout, which qwen35 uses:

$$h' = h + \mathrm{Attn}(\mathrm{Norm}_1(h))$$

$$h_{\text{out}} = h' + \mathrm{FFN}(\mathrm{Norm}_2(h'))$$

- $h$: block input of one token.
- $h'$: stream after the first residual add.
- $\mathrm{Norm}_1$: `attn_norm`; $\mathrm{Norm}_2$: `post_attention_norm` in qwen35, `ffn_norm` in many others.

Some architectures use other layouts, for example attention and FFN in parallel; this view does not tell them apart.
fullAttention.overview: A block that lets each token look back at all earlier tokens and mix in what is relevant, then refines the result with a feed-forward network.

linearAttention.detail: This view marks a block as linear attention when it holds `ssm_*` tensors, so the kind covers several designs, from Mamba-style state-space layers to qwen35's gated delta net. The mixer updates a recurrent state per token and reads its output from that state; the state does not grow with the context. In qwen35 the norms, residual adds and feed-forward network are the same as in a full-attention block.
linearAttention.math:
$$S_t = f(S_{t-1}, x_t), \qquad y_t = g(S_t, x_t)$$

- $x_t$: normed input of token $t$.
- $S_t$: recurrent state after token $t$, fixed size.
- $y_t$: mixer output, added to the residual stream.

For qwen35 the operation view shows $f$ and $g$ (gated delta rule). The block around the mixer is the same as in full attention: $h' = h + \mathrm{Mixer}(\mathrm{Norm}_1(h))$, then the FFN step.
linearAttention.overview: A block that carries a fixed-size memory from token to token instead of looking back at every earlier token. It is cheaper on long contexts, but keeps a compressed summary, not the exact past tokens.

mtp.detail: The block takes the trunk's final normed hidden state and the embedding of a token, normalizes both, joins them with `nextn.eh_proj` and runs one full-attention block, then a head norm and the LM head: `nextn.shared_head_norm` and `nextn.shared_head_head` if the file has them, else the trunk's `output_norm` and `output`. llama.cpp runs it as a separate draft graph, never inside the main forward pass.
mtp.math:
$$u = W_{eh}\,[\,\mathrm{Norm}_e(e)\,;\,\mathrm{Norm}_h(h)\,]$$

$$\ell^{\text{draft}} = W_{\text{head}}\,\mathrm{Norm}(\mathrm{Block}_{\text{full}}(u))$$

- $h$: trunk hidden state after `output_norm`.
- $e$: token embedding.
- $[\,a\,;\,b\,]$: concatenation, embedding first.
- $W_{eh}$: `nextn.eh_proj`, from width $2d$ to $d$.
- $W_{\text{head}}$: `nextn.shared_head_head`, else `output`.
- $\ell^{\text{draft}}$: logits for the draft token.
mtp.overview: An extra block that guesses one token further ahead so generation can run faster. Its guesses are drafts: the main model checks them and keeps only those it agrees with.

other.detail: The kind comes from tensor names: `nextn` means MTP, `ssm_*` means linear attention, `attn_q` or `attn_qkv` means full attention. A block with none of these lands here, for example in an architecture with its own naming.
other.math: No formula: without a template, any formula would be a guess. The tensor shapes give the sizes of the matrices the block uses.
other.overview: A block kind this view has no template for. Its tensors are read from the file, but the view does not show how they are combined.

attention.detail: Projections such as `attn_q`, `attn_k`, `attn_v` (or a fused `attn_qkv`) turn the normed input into queries, keys and values, split into heads. Keys and values of past tokens stay in the KV cache. `attn_output` maps the mixed values back to the residual width. Many models share one key/value head across several query heads (grouped-query attention).
attention.math:
$$\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_h}} + M\right) V$$

- $Q$, $K$, $V$: queries, keys and values of one head.
- $d_h$: head dimension.
- $M$: causal mask, $-\infty$ for later positions.

Heads run in parallel; their outputs are concatenated and multiplied by $W_O$ (`attn_output`). Some models use another scale than $1/\sqrt{d_h}$.
attention.overview: Lets each token gather information from earlier tokens. Each token asks a question (query), compares it with every earlier token's label (key) and takes a weighted mix of their contents (values).

embedding.detail: `token_embd` holds one row per vocabulary entry. The model looks up the row of each input token; nothing is multiplied. Some models reuse this table as the output head (tied embeddings).
embedding.math:
$$h^{(0)} = E[t]$$

- $t$: token id.
- $E$: embedding table `token_embd`, one row of width $d$ per token.
- $h^{(0)}$: residual stream entering block 0.

Some architectures scale $h^{(0)}$, for example by $\sqrt{d}$; qwen35 does not.
embedding.overview: Turns each token id into a vector of numbers, the starting point of the residual stream.

ffn.detail: Most current models use a gated form: `ffn_gate` and `ffn_up` widen the vector, the activated gate multiplies the up branch, and `ffn_down` maps back to the residual width. Older models use a plain two-layer MLP. Mixture-of-experts models route each token to a few of many such networks (router `ffn_gate_inp`).
ffn.math:
Gated form (SwiGLU when $\sigma$ is SiLU):

$$\mathrm{FFN}(x) = W_{\text{down}}\big(\sigma(W_{\text{gate}}\,x) \odot W_{\text{up}}\,x\big)$$

- $x$: normed input.
- $\sigma$: activation, SiLU in qwen35, GELU in some others.
- $\odot$: element-wise product.

Plain form: $W_{\text{down}}\,\sigma(W_{\text{up}}\,x)$, often with biases.
ffn.overview: Processes each token on its own, after attention has mixed in context. It usually holds the largest matrices of a block.

mtp.detail: Tensors under `nextn.*` (such as `eh_proj`, `enorm`, `hnorm`) plus a regular attention and FFN set. The main forward pass skips them. A runtime that supports them runs them as a draft model; others ignore them.
mtp.math:
A draft step joins the trunk state with a token embedding and predicts the following token:

$$\ell^{\text{draft}} = \mathrm{Head}\big(\mathrm{Block}(W_{eh}\,[\,\mathrm{Norm}(e)\,;\,\mathrm{Norm}(h)\,])\big)$$

- $h$: trunk hidden state.
- $e$: token embedding.
- $W_{eh}$: `nextn.eh_proj`.

A draft is kept only where the main model agrees.
mtp.overview: Extra layers that predict a token further ahead. They serve as a fast draft for speculative decoding; the main model still decides.

norm.detail: Most current models use RMSNorm; older ones use LayerNorm, which also subtracts the mean and adds a bias. The stored weight (`*_norm.weight`) has one value per dimension.
norm.math:
$$\mathrm{RMSNorm}(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}} \odot w$$

$$\mathrm{LayerNorm}(x) = \frac{x - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}} \odot w + b$$

- $n$: vector length; $\epsilon$: small constant from the file.
- $\mu$, $\sigma^2$: mean and variance of $x$.
- $w$, $b$: stored weight and bias.

qwen35 files store $w = 1 + w_{\text{HF}}$ for most norms; the Hugging Face model adds the 1 at run time.
norm.overview: Rescales a vector so its overall size stays in a stable range, then applies learned per-dimension weights. It keeps the numbers from drifting from layer to layer.

other.detail: The component is derived from the tensor name. Names the view does not know land here, for example extra projections or architecture-specific scales.
other.math: No formula: the role does not follow from the name alone.
other.overview: Tensors this view could not assign to a known component. They are read from the file; only their role is unknown here.

output.detail: `output_norm` normalizes the last block's output, then `output` (the LM head) turns it into one logit per vocabulary entry. A file without `output` reuses `token_embd` (tied weights).
output.math:
$$\ell = W_{\text{out}}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h^{(L)}), \qquad p = \mathrm{softmax}(\ell / T)$$

- $h^{(L)}$: output of the last block.
- $W_{\text{out}}$: `output`, or `token_embd` when tied.
- $\ell$: logits, one per vocabulary entry.
- $T$: sampling temperature; $p$: next-token probabilities.
output.overview: Turns the final hidden vector into a score for every token in the vocabulary. The highest scores mark the most likely next tokens.

ssm.detail: This group holds state-space and linear-attention tensors: `ssm_*`, and in qwen35 also `attn_qkv` and `attn_gate` of linear blocks. A state is carried from token to token instead of a growing KV cache.
ssm.math:
Many variants (Mamba, gated linear attention) share this form:

$$S_t = A_t \odot S_{t-1} + B_t(x_t), \qquad y_t = C_t(S_t)$$

- $S_t$: state after token $t$, fixed size.
- $A_t$: decay between 0 and 1, often input-dependent.
- $B_t$: what token $t$ writes; $C_t$: how the output reads the state.

qwen35 uses the gated delta rule, which also subtracts what the state already recalls; see the operation `delta`.
ssm.overview: A mixer that keeps a fixed-size running memory instead of looking back at every token. Each new token updates the memory and reads from it.

alpha.detail: `ssm_alpha` maps the normed input to one number per value head.
alpha.overview: Computes, per value head, the raw input for how fast the memory fades at this token.

attn.detail: Keys and values of all earlier tokens and the current one come from the KV cache, so memory grows with the context. Each key/value head serves a group of query heads. This step has no stored weight, and Model Lab does not record its weights.
attn.math:
$$a^{(j)}_t = \sum_{s \le t} \mathrm{softmax}_s\!\left(\frac{\tilde q^{(j)}_t \cdot \tilde k^{(m)}_s}{\sqrt{d_h}}\right) v^{(m)}_s$$

- $t$: current position; $s$: cached positions.
- $m$: key/value head shared by query head $j$.
- $\tilde q$, $\tilde k$: queries and keys after RoPE.
- $1/\sqrt{d_h}$: default scale; a file can set another.
attn.overview: Each query scores every cached key, the scores become weights that sum to 1, and the output is the weighted mix of the values.

attn_norm.detail: RMSNorm with the stored weight `attn_norm`, one value per dimension. Only the mixer sees the normed vector; the residual add uses the unnormed input.
attn_norm.math:
$$x = \frac{h}{\mathrm{rms}(h)} \odot w$$

- $h$: block input.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
- $w$: `attn_norm`, one weight per dimension.
attn_norm.overview: Normalizes the block input before the mixer (attention or linear attention).

attn_residual.detail: The unnormed block input plus the mixer's output projection. The sum feeds the norm before the feed-forward network and is kept for the second residual add.
attn_residual.math:
$$h' = h + y$$

- $h$: block input.
- $y$: mixer output (`attn_output` or `ssm_out`).
attn_residual.overview: Adds the mixer's result to the block input. The block adds to the stream; it never replaces it.

beta.detail: `ssm_beta` maps the normed input to one number per value head; a sigmoid squeezes it into the range 0 to 1.
beta.overview: Computes, per value head, how strongly this token writes into the memory.

concat.detail: The embedding comes first, then the hidden state. No stored weight.
concat.overview: Joins the normed embedding and the normed hidden state into one vector of twice the width.

control_vector.detail: llama.cpp can load a control vector: one direction per layer, already scaled by the chosen strength, added to every token's block output for the layers in its range; block 0 never gets one. It is not part of the model file. Model Lab traces run on the Hugging Face checkpoint, so they never include it.
control_vector.math:
$$h_{\text{out}} = h'' + c_i$$

- $h''$: output of the FFN residual add.
- $c_i$: control vector for block $i$; $0$ when none is loaded and always for block 0.
control_vector.overview: Adds a fixed steering vector for this layer when one is loaded. Without one, nothing changes.

conv.detail: `ssm_conv1d` is a depthwise causal convolution over the query, key and value channels: each channel has its own short kernel and sees only the current and earlier tokens. The recent inputs are kept as conv state between tokens. SiLU follows.
conv.math:
$$c_t[i] = \mathrm{SiLU}\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{K-1} w[i,j]\; m_{t-K+1+j}[i]\Big)$$

- $m_t$: output of `attn_qkv` at token $t$.
- $i$: channel; $K$: kernel size.
- $w$: `ssm_conv1d`, no bias.
- $\mathrm{SiLU}(u) = u \cdot \mathrm{sigmoid}(u)$.
conv.overview: Mixes each channel with its values from the last few tokens, so the mixer sees a little local context.

decay.detail: Adds the learned bias `ssm_dt`, applies softplus and multiplies by `ssm_a`, which the converter stores as minus the exponential of `A_log`. The result is negative, so its exponential lies between 0 and 1. A larger α means faster forgetting.
decay.math:
$$g_t = -\exp(A_{\log}) \cdot \mathrm{softplus}(a_t + b_{dt}), \qquad \gamma_t = e^{g_t}$$

- $a_t$: output of `ssm_alpha`.
- $b_{dt}$: `ssm_dt`.
- $-\exp(A_{\log})$: `ssm_a` as stored.
- $\mathrm{softplus}(u) = \ln(1 + e^u)$.
- $\gamma_t \in (0,1)$: factor the state is multiplied by.
decay.overview: Turns α into a forget factor between 0 and 1: how much of the old memory each value head keeps at this token.

delta.detail: Each value head keeps a state matrix (key-head size by value-head size) that is carried from token to token and does not grow with the context. The state is not stored in the file; it exists only while text is processed.
delta.math:
$$S' = \gamma_t\,S_{t-1}, \qquad S_t = S' + \beta_t\,\hat k_t\big(v_t - S'^{\top}\hat k_t\big)^{\top}$$

$$o_t = S_t^{\top}\,\hat q_t / \sqrt{d_k}$$

- $S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d_v}$: state of one value head.
- $\gamma_t$, $\beta_t$: decay factor and write strength of that head.
- $\hat q_t$, $\hat k_t$: L2-normed query and key; $v_t$: value.
- $o_t$: output of the head.

This is the per-token form; a prompt is processed in chunks with the same result up to rounding.
delta.overview: The memory step. The state first fades by the decay factor, then is corrected toward this token: it replaces what it would recall for this key with the token's value, by the write strength β.

eh_proj.detail: `nextn.eh_proj` maps twice the model width back to `n_embd`. Its output is the MTP block's residual stream: it feeds `attn_norm` and the first residual add.
eh_proj.math:
$$u = W_{eh}\,c$$

- $c$: output of the concatenation.
- $W_{eh}$: `nextn.eh_proj`, from $2d$ to $d$.
eh_proj.overview: Mixes the joined vector back down to the model width.

enorm.overview: Normalizes the token embedding before it is joined with the trunk hidden state.

exp_act.detail: SiLU on each chosen expert's gate branch, multiplied element-wise by its up branch (SwiGLU), separately for every chosen expert. No stored weight.
exp_act.math:
$$m_e = \mathrm{SiLU}(g_e) \odot u_e, \qquad e \in S$$

- $g_e$, $u_e$: expert $e$'s gate and up branches.
- $\mathrm{SiLU}(z) = z \cdot \mathrm{sigmoid}(z)$.
- $S$: the chosen experts.
exp_act.overview: Combines each chosen expert's two branches, as a dense feed-forward network does.

exp_down.detail: `ffn_down_exps` stacks one down matrix per expert (`mlp.experts.down_proj` in the Hugging Face checkpoint); only the chosen experts' matrices are used. The result is still one vector per chosen expert; the router weights are applied next.
exp_down.math:
$$E_e(x') = W_{d,e}\,m_e, \qquad e \in S$$

- $m_e$: expert $e$'s SiLU product.
- $W_{d,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_down_exps`, from the expert width $d_{\text{exp}}$ to $d$.

Per expert: $E_e(x) = W_{d,e}\big(\mathrm{SiLU}(W_{g,e}\,x) \odot W_{u,e}\,x\big)$.
exp_down.overview: Maps each chosen expert's wide vector back to the residual width.

exp_gate.detail: `ffn_gate_exps` stacks one gate matrix per expert in one tensor; only the matrices of the chosen experts are used for this token. Some files store gate and up together as `ffn_gate_up_exps`; this node is then the logical gate half of that tensor, computed the same way. In the Hugging Face checkpoint the gate rows are the first half of `mlp.experts.gate_up_proj`.
exp_gate.math:
$$g_e = W_{g,e}\,x', \qquad e \in S$$

- $x'$: output of the norm before the FFN; every chosen expert reads the same $x'$.
- $W_{g,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_gate_exps` (or the gate half of `ffn_gate_up_exps`), from $d$ to the expert width $d_{\text{exp}}$.
- $S$: the chosen experts.
exp_gate.overview: Each chosen expert widens the normed vector into its own gate branch.

exp_up.detail: `ffn_up_exps` stacks one up matrix per expert; only the chosen experts' matrices are used, from the same input as the gate. When the file stores `ffn_gate_up_exps`, this node is the logical up half of that tensor. In the Hugging Face checkpoint the up rows are the second half of `mlp.experts.gate_up_proj`.
exp_up.math:
$$u_e = W_{u,e}\,x', \qquad e \in S$$

- $W_{u,e}$: expert $e$'s slice of `ffn_up_exps` (or the up half of `ffn_gate_up_exps`), from $d$ to $d_{\text{exp}}$.
- $S$: the chosen experts.
exp_up.overview: Each chosen expert widens the normed vector into its own up branch.

exp_weighted.detail: Each chosen expert's output is multiplied by its router weight, and the results are added. llama.cpp applies the weights after the down projection; because that projection is linear, weighting earlier would give the same sum. Experts that were not chosen contribute nothing.
exp_weighted.math:
$$y_{\text{routed}} = \sum_{e \in S} w_e\, E_e(x')$$

- $S$: the chosen experts; $w_e$: their weights.
- $E_e(x')$: expert $e$'s output after `ffn_down_exps`.
exp_weighted.overview: Mixes the chosen experts' outputs, each scaled by its router weight.

ffn_act.detail: SiLU on the gate branch, multiplied element-wise by the up branch (SwiGLU). No stored weight.
ffn_act.overview: Combines the two branches: the activated gate decides how much of each up-branch value passes.

ffn_down.math:
$$f = W_{\text{down}}\,m$$

- $m$: output of the SiLU product.
- $W_{\text{down}}$: `ffn_down`, from $d_{ff}$ to $d$.
ffn_down.overview: Maps the wide vector back to the residual width.

ffn_gate.detail: `ffn_gate` maps width `n_embd` to the FFN width `n_ff`.
ffn_gate.math:
$$g = W_{\text{gate}}\,x'$$

- $x'$: output of the norm before the FFN.
- $W_{\text{gate}}$: `ffn_gate`, from $d$ to $d_{ff}$.
ffn_gate.overview: Widens the normed vector into the gate branch of the feed-forward network.

ffn_residual.detail: The unnormed sum from the first residual add plus the `ffn_down` output. In a trunk block this is the block output unless a control vector is loaded; in the MTP block it goes to the head norm.
ffn_residual.math:
$$h'' = h' + f$$

- $h'$: output of the first residual add.
- $f$: output of `ffn_down`.
ffn_residual.overview: Adds the feed-forward result to the stream.

ffn_up.detail: `ffn_up` maps `n_embd` to `n_ff`, in parallel with `ffn_gate` and from the same input.
ffn_up.overview: Widens the normed vector into the value branch of the feed-forward network.

gate.detail: A sigmoid on the second half of each head's Q output (`attn_q`, or the Q rows of `attn_qkv`). One factor per output dimension lets the model damp or pass each part of the attention result for this token.
gate.math:
$$\sigma^{(j)} = \mathrm{sigmoid}(g^{(j)}) \in (0,1)^{d_h}$$

- $g^{(j)}$: gate half of head $j$ from `attn_q` or the Q rows of `attn_qkv`.
gate.overview: Turns the gate half of the query projection into factors between 0 and 1.

gated.detail: Each head's attention output is scaled by its sigmoid gate before the output projection.
gated.math:
$$\bar a^{(j)} = a^{(j)} \odot \sigma^{(j)}$$

- $a^{(j)}$: attention output of head $j$.
- $\sigma^{(j)}$: its gate.
gated.overview: Multiplies the attention output by the gate, element by element.

gated_norm.detail: RMSNorm per value head with `ssm_norm` (one weight per head dimension, shared by all heads, stored without the +1), then an element-wise product with SiLU of the `attn_gate` output.
gated_norm.math:
$$y_t = \frac{o_t}{\mathrm{rms}(o_t)} \odot w \odot \mathrm{SiLU}(z_t)$$

- $o_t$: delta-rule output of one head, length $d_v$.
- $w$: `ssm_norm`.
- $z_t$: that head's slice of the `attn_gate` output.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
gated_norm.overview: Normalizes each head's memory output and scales it by the output gate z.

head.detail: Uses `nextn.shared_head_head` when present, else the trunk's LM head `output`, which may itself be tied to `token_embd`.
head.math:
$$\ell^{\text{draft}} = W_{\text{head}}\,z$$

- $z$: output of the head norm.
- $W_{\text{head}}$: `nextn.shared_head_head`, else `output`.
head.overview: Turns the normed MTP state into a score per vocabulary entry.

head_norm.detail: RMSNorm with `nextn.shared_head_norm` when the file has it, else with the trunk's `output_norm`.
head_norm.math:
$$z = \frac{h''}{\mathrm{rms}(h'')} \odot w$$

- $h''$: output of the MTP block's FFN residual add.
- $w$: `nextn.shared_head_norm`, else `output_norm`.
head_norm.overview: Normalizes the MTP block's output before its head.

hidden.detail: It is the same normed vector the LM head reads.
hidden.math:
$$h = \frac{h^{(L)}}{\mathrm{rms}(h^{(L)})} \odot w_{\text{out}}$$

- $h^{(L)}$: output of the last trunk block.
- $w_{\text{out}}$: `output_norm`.
hidden.overview: The trunk's final hidden state, after the last block and `output_norm`, handed to the MTP block.

hnorm.overview: Normalizes the trunk hidden state before it is joined with the token embedding.

input.detail: For block 0 it is the token embedding; for any later block it is the previous block's output. It feeds `attn_norm` and, unchanged, the first residual add.
input.math:
$$h^{(i)} = h_{\text{out}}^{(i-1)}, \qquad h^{(0)} = E[t]$$

- $h^{(i)}$: input of block $i$ for one token.
- $E[t]$: embedding row of token $t$.
input.overview: The vector this block receives: the running sum of everything the embedding and earlier blocks have added (the residual stream).

k.detail: `attn_k` (or the K rows of a fused `attn_qkv`) produces one key per key/value head. There can be fewer key/value heads than query heads (grouped-query attention); each serves a group of query heads. Keys go into the KV cache after RoPE.
k.math:
$$k = W_K\,x + b_K$$

- $W_K$: `attn_k`, or the K rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_{kv} d_h$.
- $b_K$: `attn_k.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the K entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_k.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise.
- $n_{kv}$: number of key/value heads.
k.overview: Projects the normed input into keys, the labels that queries are compared with.

k_norm.detail: RMSNorm over the head dimension with `attn_k_norm`: one weight per head dimension, shared by all key heads, stored as 1 plus the Hugging Face value.
k_norm.math:
$$\tilde k^{(m)} = \frac{k^{(m)}}{\mathrm{rms}(k^{(m)})} \odot w_k$$

- $k^{(m)}$: key head $m$, length $d_h$.
- $w_k$: `attn_k_norm`.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
k_norm.overview: Normalizes each key head before the position encoding.

l2_norm.detail: Applied per head to queries and keys, not to values. No stored weight. Unit-length keys keep the delta-rule update well scaled.
l2_norm.math:
$$\hat q = \frac{q}{\lVert q \rVert_2}, \qquad \hat k = \frac{k}{\lVert k \rVert_2}$$

- $q$, $k$: one query or key head.
- $\lVert u \rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_i u_i^2}$; a small $\epsilon$ guards against division by zero.
l2_norm.overview: Scales each query and key head to length 1, so only its direction counts.

logits.detail: These logits only propose. In speculative decoding the main model evaluates the draft in its next pass and keeps it only where it agrees, so a rejected draft costs time but does not change what the main model would produce: exactly so for greedy decoding, in distribution when sampling.
logits.math:
$$p^{\text{draft}} = \mathrm{softmax}(\ell^{\text{draft}})$$

- $\ell^{\text{draft}}$: draft logits, one per vocabulary entry.
- $p^{\text{draft}}$: draft probabilities; the runtime's speculative settings decide how a draft is picked.
logits.overview: Scores for the draft token. A draft is picked from them, and the main model then checks it.

mixer_out.detail: `attn_output` takes the concatenated heads and mixes them into one vector of width `n_embd`.
mixer_out.math:
$$y = W_O\,[\,a^{(1)};\dots;a^{(n_h)}\,]$$

- $a^{(j)}$: attention output of query head $j$.
- $W_O$: `attn_output`, from $n_h d_h$ to $d$.
mixer_out.overview: Maps the attention output of all heads back to the residual width.

moe_out.detail: The routed mix plus the gated shared expert takes the place of a dense FFN's `ffn_down` output and goes to the second residual add. For each token only the k chosen experts and the shared expert did any work; the other experts' weights were not read.
moe_out.math:
$$y = \sum_{e \in S} w_e\, E_e(x') + \mathrm{sigmoid}\big(g^{\top} x'\big)\, E_{\text{sh}}(x')$$

$$p = \mathrm{softmax}(W_r\,x'), \qquad S = \mathrm{TopK}_k(p), \qquad E(x) = W_d\big(\mathrm{SiLU}(W_g\,x) \odot W_u\,x\big)$$

- $W_r$: the router `ffn_gate_inp`; $w_e$: the chosen experts' weights.
- $g$: `ffn_gate_inp_shexp`; $E_{\text{sh}}$: the shared expert.
moe_out.overview: Adds the routed experts' mix and the gated shared expert: the feed-forward result of this block.

output.detail: Same width as the input. The next block reads it as its input; after the last block, `output_norm` and the LM head turn it into logits. Model Lab traces measure this vector, without a control vector.
output.math:
$$h^{(i+1)} = h_{\text{out}}^{(i)}$$

After the last block: $\ell = W_{\text{out}}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h^{(L)})$.

- $\ell$: logits; $W_{\text{out}}$: `output`, or `token_embd` when tied.
output.overview: What the block passes on: the updated residual stream.

post_norm.detail: RMSNorm with its own stored weight, one value per dimension, called `ffn_norm` in many architectures. It is a pre-norm for the FFN: the residual add uses the unnormed sum.
post_norm.math:
$$x' = \frac{h'}{\mathrm{rms}(h')} \odot w$$

- $h'$: output of the first residual add.
- $w$: the FFN norm's weight (`ffn_norm` in many architectures).
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
post_norm.overview: Normalizes the stream again before the feed-forward network.

q.detail: `attn_q` (or the Q rows of a fused `attn_qkv`) produces one query per head, all heads side by side in one vector. Queries are compared with the cached keys; they are not cached themselves.
q.math:
$$q = W_Q\,x + b_Q$$

- $W_Q$: `attn_q`, or the Q rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_h d_h$.
- $b_Q$: `attn_q.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the Q entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_q.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise.
- $n_h$: number of query heads; $d_h$: head size.
q.overview: Projects the normed input into queries: what each token looks for among the tokens it attends to.

q_norm.detail: RMSNorm over the head dimension with `attn_q_norm`: one weight per head dimension, shared by all heads, stored as 1 plus the Hugging Face value.
q_norm.math:
$$\tilde q^{(j)} = \frac{q^{(j)}}{\mathrm{rms}(q^{(j)})} \odot w_q$$

- $q^{(j)}$: query head $j$, length $d_h$.
- $w_q$: `attn_q_norm`.
- $\mathrm{rms}(u) = \sqrt{\mathrm{mean}(u^2) + \epsilon}$, $\epsilon$ from the file.
q_norm.overview: Normalizes each query head before the position encoding.

qkv.detail: `attn_qkv` produces queries and keys for the key heads and values for the value heads, in one vector. The result passes the causal convolution before it is split.
qkv.math:
$$m_t = W_{qkv}\,x_t$$

- $x_t$: output of `attn_norm`.
- $W_{qkv}$: `attn_qkv`, output length $2 n_k d_k + n_v d_v$.
- $n_k$, $d_k$: key head count and size; $n_v$, $d_v$: value head count and size.
qkv.overview: Projects the normed input into queries, keys and values for the linear-attention mixer, with one matrix.

rope.detail: Applied to the queries and keys, not to values; no stored weight. The base frequency, the number of rotated dimensions and any context scaling come from the file's metadata.
rope.math:
$$\begin{pmatrix} u'_{i_1} \\ u'_{i_2} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos p\theta_i & -\sin p\theta_i \\ \sin p\theta_i & \cos p\theta_i \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_{i_1} \\ u_{i_2} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \theta_i = b^{-i/r}$$

- $u$: one query or key head; pair $i < r$ rotates its dimensions $i_1$ and $i_2$.
- Which two dimensions form a pair depends on the model: neighbours ($i_1 = 2i$, $i_2 = 2i + 1$) or the two halves ($i_1 = i$, $i_2 = i + r$).
- $2r$: number of rotated dimensions; the rest pass unchanged.
- $b$: base frequency; $p$: position.

The score $\langle R_p q, R_s k \rangle$ then depends on $p$ and $s$ only through $p - s$.
rope.overview: Encodes each token's position by rotating pairs of query and key values by an angle that grows with the position. The attention score then depends on how far apart two tokens are.

router.detail: `ffn_gate_inp` has one row per expert (`mlp.gate.weight` in the Hugging Face checkpoint). Its product with the normed vector gives one logit per expert; nothing is chosen yet. Files usually keep it unquantized: it is small, and it decides which experts run.
router.math:
$$z = W_r\,x'$$

- $x'$: output of the norm before the FFN.
- $W_r$: `ffn_gate_inp`, from $d$ to $n_{\text{exp}}$, one row per expert.
- $z$: router logits, one per expert.
router.overview: Scores every expert for this token: one logit per expert, from the normed input.

router_probs.detail: A softmax over every expert, not only the ones that will be chosen, so the probabilities of all experts add up to 1. Both the choice and the weights of the chosen experts start from these probabilities.
router_probs.math:
$$p_e = \frac{\exp(z_e)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n_{\text{exp}}} \exp(z_j)}$$

- $z$: router logits; $e$: expert index.
- $n_{\text{exp}}$: number of experts in the block.
- $\sum_e p_e = 1$ over all experts.
router_probs.overview: Turns the router logits into probabilities over all experts.

shexp_act.detail: SiLU on the shared expert's gate branch, multiplied element-wise by its up branch (SwiGLU). No stored weight.
shexp_act.overview: Combines the shared expert's two branches.

shexp_down.detail: `ffn_down_shexp` (`mlp.shared_expert.down_proj` in the Hugging Face checkpoint). Its output is scaled by the shared expert's gate before it joins the routed experts.
shexp_down.math:
$$E_{\text{sh}}(x') = W_{d,\text{sh}}\,m_{\text{sh}}$$

- $m_{\text{sh}}$: the shared expert's SiLU product.
- $W_{d,\text{sh}}$: `ffn_down_shexp`, from the shared expert's width to $d$.
shexp_down.overview: Maps the shared expert's wide vector back to the residual width.

shexp_gate.detail: Besides the routed experts, this block has a shared expert: an ordinary gated feed-forward network that every token passes through, whatever the router picked. `ffn_gate_shexp` is its gate projection (`mlp.shared_expert.gate_proj` in the Hugging Face checkpoint).
shexp_gate.math:
$$g_{\text{sh}} = W_{g,\text{sh}}\,x'$$

- $x'$: output of the norm before the FFN.
- $W_{g,\text{sh}}$: `ffn_gate_shexp`, from $d$ to the shared expert's width.
shexp_gate.overview: The shared expert, which runs for every token, widens the normed vector into its gate branch.

shexp_gated.detail: The shared expert's output, multiplied by the single factor from its gate. No stored weight.
shexp_gated.math:
$$y_{\text{sh}} = s\, E_{\text{sh}}(x')$$

- $s$: the shared expert's gate.
- $E_{\text{sh}}(x')$: output of `ffn_down_shexp`.
shexp_gated.overview: Scales the shared expert's output by its gate.

shexp_scale.detail: `ffn_gate_inp_shexp` is a single vector (`mlp.shared_expert_gate.weight` in the Hugging Face checkpoint). Its dot product with the normed input, passed through a sigmoid, gives one factor for the whole shared-expert output. Unlike the router it chooses nothing; it only scales.
shexp_scale.math:
$$s = \mathrm{sigmoid}\big(g^{\top} x'\big) \in (0, 1)$$

- $g$: `ffn_gate_inp_shexp`, one value per dimension.
- $x'$: output of the norm before the FFN.
shexp_scale.overview: Decides for each token how much of the shared expert's output is used: one number between 0 and 1.

shexp_up.detail: `ffn_up_shexp` (`mlp.shared_expert.up_proj` in the Hugging Face checkpoint) widens the normed input in parallel with the shared expert's gate projection.
shexp_up.math:
$$u_{\text{sh}} = W_{u,\text{sh}}\,x'$$

- $W_{u,\text{sh}}$: `ffn_up_shexp`, from $d$ to the shared expert's width.
shexp_up.overview: Widens the normed vector into the shared expert's up branch.

split.detail: The first part gives the queries, the next the keys, the rest the values, each reshaped into heads. When there are fewer key heads than value heads, each query and key head serves several value heads.
split.math:
$$c_t = [\,q_t\,;\,k_t\,;\,v_t\,]$$

- $q_t, k_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_k d_k}$: queries and keys, in heads of size $d_k$.
- $v_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n_v d_v}$: values, in heads of size $d_v$.
split.overview: Cuts the convolved vector into queries, keys and values.

token.detail: Looked up in `nextn.embed_tokens` when the file has it, else in the shared `token_embd`.
token.overview: The embedding of a token, the second input of the MTP block: the token the trunk has just produced.

topk.detail: The `n_expert_used` experts with the largest probabilities are kept (k, from the file's metadata); the others are skipped for this token. That is why a mixture-of-experts model computes only a fraction of its weights per token. The choice is per token and per block: the next token, or the next block, can pick other experts.
topk.math:
$$S = \mathrm{TopK}_k(p) \subset \{1, \dots, n_{\text{exp}}\}, \qquad |S| = k$$

- $p$: router probabilities.
- $k$: `n_expert_used` from the file's metadata.
- Experts outside $S$ are not computed for this token.
topk.overview: Picks the experts with the highest probabilities; only these run for this token.

topk_weights.detail: Each chosen expert gets its router probability as its weight. Some architectures then divide these by their sum, so the chosen weights add up to 1; others keep them as they are, so they add up to less than 1. Which one applies is a property of the architecture.
topk_weights.math:
$$w_e = p_e \quad \text{or} \quad w_e = \frac{p_e}{\sum_{j \in S} p_j}, \qquad e \in S$$

- $p_e$: router probability of expert $e$; $S$: the chosen experts.
- The second form renormalizes the chosen probabilities to add up to 1; the architecture decides which form applies.
topk_weights.overview: The weights the chosen experts' outputs are mixed with, taken from the router probabilities.

v.detail: `attn_v` (or the V rows of a fused `attn_qkv`) produces one value per key/value head. Values get no norm and no RoPE; they go into the KV cache as they are.
v.math:
$$v = W_V\,x + b_V$$

- $W_V$: `attn_v`, or the V rows of `attn_qkv`; output length $n_{kv} d_h$.
- $b_V$: `attn_v.bias` (separate weights); with a fused `attn_qkv`, the V entries of `attn_qkv.bias`, or `attn_v.bias` only when all three Q/K/V biases exist; zero otherwise.
v.overview: Projects the normed input into values, the content a token passes on when it is attended to.

z.detail: `attn_gate` gives one gate value per value-head dimension. It acts at the end, in the gated norm.
z.math:
$$z_t = W_z\,x_t$$

- $x_t$: output of `attn_norm`.
- $W_z$: `attn_gate`, output length $n_v d_v$.
z.overview: Projects the normed input into an output gate that later scales the mixer's result.

mixer_out.detail: `ssm_out` takes the concatenated heads from the gated norm and produces the linear-attention contribution.
mixer_out.math:
$$y = W_{\text{out}}\,[\,y^{(1)};\dots;y^{(n_v)}\,]$$

- $y^{(j)}$: gated-norm output of value head $j$.
- $W_{\text{out}}$: `ssm_out`, from $n_v d_v$ to $d$.
mixer_out.overview: Maps the gated memory output of all value heads back to the residual width.

attn_residual.detail: In the MTP block the residual starts at the `nextn.eh_proj` output, not at a trunk block's output. The sum feeds `post_attention_norm` and is kept for the second residual add.
attn_residual.math:
$$h' = u + y$$

- $u$: output of `nextn.eh_proj`.
- $y$: output of `attn_output`.
attn_residual.overview: Adds the attention result to the MTP block's own stream, the `nextn.eh_proj` output.

attentionMap.detail: Columns are the key positions that hold a stored weight for this block and head in any step, in position order; beyond 256 columns, the ones with the largest summed weight stay and a note counts the rest. The color scale runs from 0 to the largest weight in view, named in the legend, so colors do not compare across heads or blocks. Four cell states are drawn apart from the shaded weights: future position (the key comes after the query, so causal attention cannot read it), not in the top K (not stored; its weight is part of the row's rest), floored to 0 (stored, but below 1/10,000) and row missing (the run dropped this step's row at its size limit). A bright column through many rows is often an attention sink on a template or first token, not a sign of relevance. The key list holds the same values for the current row.
attentionMap.math:
$$M_{s,c} = a^{(j)}_{P+s-1,\,c}$$

- $s$: generated token (row); $c$: key position (column); $j$: the chosen head.
- Future position: $c > P+s-1$; the causal mask makes $a = 0$.
- Not in the top K: $c \notin \mathcal{K}$ of that row; the weight is unknown and counted in the rest.
- Floored to 0: $c \in \mathcal{K}$ with $a < 10^{-4}$.
- Color: $M_{s,c} / \max M$ over the cells in view.
attentionMap.overview: The map stacks the rows of all steps: one row per generated token, one column per key position. A darker cell means more weight; the current step's row is marked.

attentionRow.detail: The query belongs to the position the step reads, so the row of generated token $s$ covers key positions 0 to $P+s-1$. A weight shows where the head reads from, not what it writes: the values are mixed by these weights, then the output projection (in Qwen3.5 after a gate per dimension) decides how much reaches the residual stream, so a large weight on a small or gated-off value changes little. Attention is therefore neither an explanation nor an importance score. Template tokens and the first token often take a large share (attention sinks); a high weight there says nothing about relevant content. The weights are recomputed in fp32 from the query and key tensors the kernel used; only the top keys are kept, rounded down to 1/10,000.
attentionRow.math:
$$a^{(j)}_{t,s} = \frac{\exp\big(\tilde q^{(j)}_t \cdot \tilde k^{(m)}_s / \sqrt{d_h}\big)}{\sum_{u \le t} \exp\big(\tilde q^{(j)}_t \cdot \tilde k^{(m)}_u / \sqrt{d_h}\big)}, \qquad s \le t$$

$$o^{(j)}_t = \mathrm{sigmoid}\big(g^{(j)}_t\big) \odot \sum_{s \le t} a^{(j)}_{t,s}\, v^{(m)}_s \;\; (\text{Qwen3.5}), \qquad o^{(j)}_t = \sum_{s \le t} a^{(j)}_{t,s}\, v^{(m)}_s \;\; (\text{OLMoE})$$

$$y_t = W_O\big[o^{(1)}_t; \dots; o^{(H)}_t\big]$$

- $t$: query position; $s$: key position; $j$: query head; $m$: the key/value head of its group.
- Qwen3.5: $\tilde q = \mathrm{RoPE}(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(q))$, $\tilde k$ likewise: RMSNorm per head (`q_norm`, `k_norm`), then RoPE on the first part of each head only; the checkpoint config sets that share.
- OLMoE: $\tilde q = \mathrm{RoPE}(\mathrm{clip}_c(\mathrm{RMSNorm}(q)))$, $\tilde k$ likewise: RMSNorm over the whole projection, all heads at once (`q_norm`, `k_norm`), then, when the config sets `clip_qkv` $= c$, every value clamped to $[-c, c]$ (the values $v$ too), then RoPE on the full head.
- $d_h$: head dimension; both families scale by exactly $1/\sqrt{d_h}$.
- $g^{(j)}_t$: gate half of the query projection, Qwen3.5 only; OLMoE has no gate. $W_O$: `o_proj`.

The row shown is $a^{(j)}_{t,\cdot}$; the values, any gate and $W_O$ act after it and are not recorded.
attentionRow.overview: For the chosen step, block and head, this row shows how the head's query spread its weight over all earlier positions and its own. Each weight lies between 0 and 1, and the row adds up to 1.

heads.detail: The checkpoint config sets the head counts. With grouped-query attention, several query heads share one key/value head: they compare against the same keys, but with their own queries, so their rows still differ. The default Qwen3.5 config, for example, has 16 query heads sharing 4 key/value heads (groups of 4) and a full-attention block every 4th block; OLMoE-1B-7B has 16 query heads and 16 key/value heads (groups of 1, so every head has its own keys) and full attention in every block. The run states the values of this checkpoint. A recorded block stores all of its query heads. Head numbers are positions in the model, not a ranking; this view does not rate any head as important.
heads.math:
$$G = H / H_{kv}, \qquad j = m\,G + g, \quad 0 \le g < G$$

- $H$: query heads; $H_{kv}$: key/value heads; $G$: query heads per group.
- Query head $j$ reads key/value head $m = \lfloor j / G \rfloor$.
- Heads of one group share $\tilde k^{(m)}$ and $v^{(m)}$ and differ in $\tilde q^{(j)}$ (and, in Qwen3.5, in their gate).
- At $G = 1$ (OLMoE) each group is one head, so $m = j$.

All $H$ head outputs are concatenated before $W_O$, so what one head contributes also depends on $W_O$.
heads.overview: Attention runs as several heads side by side, each with its own query and its own weights. You view one head at a time; different heads can look at very different positions.

lens.detail: For each generated step, the run keeps every block's output at the position the step reads passes the blocks before the last through the final RMSNorm and the output projection (`lm_head`) in one batched call, takes the last block's row straight from the model's own output logits, then applies one softmax over the whole vocabulary. The modules are the model's own, so the norm's effective weight $\gamma$ ($1 + w$ in Qwen3.5, $w$ in OLMoE), its float32 arithmetic and any weight sharing with the token embeddings are exactly those of the real readout. The lens uses the raw logits; the checkpoint's generation settings do not apply to it. Each block keeps its top N tokens (the run states N), the chosen token's log-probability and rank, and the readout's spread; log-probabilities are rounded down to 1/10,000. At the last block the lens is the model's own output; at every earlier block it is the final readout applied early, which the model never does. The vocabulary size V comes from the checkpoint (about 248k tokens for Qwen3.5, for example).
lens.math:
$$p^{(b)}_t = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W_U\, \mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(h^{(b)}_t)\big), \qquad \mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(x) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_i x_i^2 + \epsilon}} \odot \gamma$$

- $h^{(b)}_t$: output of block $b$ at position $t = P+s-1$, the position step $s$ reads; $b = 0, \dots, B-1$.
- $W_U \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d}$: the output projection (`lm_head`), without bias; whether it equals the token embedding matrix depends on the checkpoint config.
- $\gamma$: the final norm's effective weight, $1 + w$ in Qwen3.5 and $w$ in OLMoE, where $w$ is its stored weight; $\epsilon$: its epsilon. The norm normalizes in float32 and returns bf16; the logits stay bf16, softmax runs in float32.
- $B$, $d$ (hidden size) and $V$ come from the checkpoint.
- The lens always runs the checkpoint's own norm module, so $\gamma$ is the family's own.

At $b = B-1$ this is the model's output: $W_U\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(h^{(B-1)}_t) = \ell^{(s)}$. For $b < B-1$ it is a readout the model never computes.
lens.overview: The logit lens reads every block's output at this step through the model's own final norm and output projection, as if the model stopped after that block. It shows which tokens that early readout favours. It is a derived analysis computed beside the run, not what the model computed: only the last block's output reached the output layer.

lensCaveats.detail: Four limits apply. Only the last block's output reaches the output layer in the real model; the other readouts are computed beside the run and never influence a token. Early blocks' states are not yet in the basis the output projection reads, so low agreement with the chosen token and high spread there are expected and say little. When the checkpoint shares the output projection with the token embeddings (the run says whether it does), the first blocks tend to echo the token at the current position, because their state is still close to that token's embedding. And this is the plain readout, not a tuned lens: no block gets a learned translation into the output basis, so a block can hold information the lens cannot show. A high lens probability is therefore no proof that a block "decided" or "knows" anything, and a low one no proof that it does not.
lensCaveats.math:
$$h^{(b)}_t = e_{x_t} + \sum_{j=0}^{b} \Delta^{(j)}_t, \qquad \ell^{(b)}_v = e_v^{\top}\, \mathrm{RMSNorm}_f\big(h^{(b)}_t\big) \;\; (W_U = E)$$

- $e_{x_t}$: embedding of the token read at position $t$; $\Delta^{(j)}_t$: what block $j$ adds to the residual stream.
- With tied weights, row $v$ of $W_U$ is token $v$'s embedding $e_v$; while $h^{(b)}_t$ is still close to $e_{x_t}$, the logit of $v = x_t$ tends to be large.
- No readout for $b < B-1$ enters generation; each token comes from $\ell^{(s)}$ alone.
lensCaveats.overview: A lens readout is the model's final readout applied early, not what the model "thinks" at that block. It is a derived analysis: computed from measured states, but not something the model computed or used for its decision.

lensChosen.detail: The chosen token is the one the trace generated: the top candidate after the checkpoint's generation settings. The lens reads raw logits, so even at the last block its rank can be greater than 1 when those settings changed the order. Rank 1 means no token has a higher lens probability. Tokens with exactly the same value share the better rank, so the chosen token can be rank 1 while another token is listed first; the view then says "tied for first". When the token is outside a block's top N, the view still shows its rank and probability, which the run stores separately. The shown probability comes from the log-probability rounded down, so it never exceeds the computed one. A probability that rises across the blocks shows where the final readout would start to pick this token; it does not show that a block decided anything.
lensChosen.math:
$$\pi^{(b)} = p^{(b)}_{t,x}, \qquad r^{(b)} = 1 + \big|\{\, v : p^{(b)}_{t,v} > p^{(b)}_{t,x} \,\}\big|$$

- $x = x_{P+s}$: the token generated at step $s$; $p^{(b)}_t$: the lens distribution of block $b$.
- $r^{(b)}$: competition rank; equal values share the better rank, so $r^{(b)} = 1$ does not exclude a tie.
- Stored: $\lambda^{(b)} = \ln \pi^{(b)}$, rounded down to a multiple of $10^{-4}$; shown: $e^{\lambda^{(b)}} \le \pi^{(b)}$.
lensChosen.overview: For every block, this column shows the probability and rank its lens readout gives the token the model actually chose at this step. Read down the blocks to see from which depth the final readout would pick it; that is not where the model decided.

lensEntropy.detail: The spread is the entropy of the block's lens distribution over the whole vocabulary, computed in float32 and stored to three decimals. Its unit is the nat because it uses the natural logarithm, like every log-probability here. $e^H$ turns it into a count: a readout with spread $H$ is about as spread as $e^H$ equally likely tokens, so about 0.69 nats is like a coin flip between two and 2.30 nats like a choice among ten. The maximum is $\ln V$, reached only when all V tokens are equally likely. High spread at early blocks is expected for a lens: their states are not yet in the basis the output projection reads, so the final readout applied there often gives a flat distribution. The spread describes that readout, not the model's uncertainty at that block. A low spread does not mean correct either: a readout can be sharp on a token the model does not choose. At the last block it is the spread of the raw output, before the generation settings. "–" marks a value that was not a finite number.
lensEntropy.math:
$$H^{(b)} = -\sum_{v=1}^{V} p^{(b)}_{t,v} \ln p^{(b)}_{t,v}, \qquad 0 \le H^{(b)} \le \ln V, \qquad k^{(b)} = e^{H^{(b)}}$$

- $p^{(b)}_{t,v}$: lens probability of token $v$ at block $b$; a term with $p = 0$ counts as 0.
- $H = 0$: one token has probability 1; $H = \ln V$: all $V$ tokens are equally likely.
- $k^{(b)}$: the number of equally likely tokens with the same entropy, since $k$ of them give exactly $\ln k$.
- Unit nats; in bits it would be $H / \ln 2$.

Example: with the roughly 248k tokens of Qwen3.5, $\ln V \approx 12.42$; the view computes the bound from this checkpoint's $V$.
lensEntropy.overview: The spread says how evenly one block's lens readout shares out its probability. 0 nats means one token takes all of it; the higher the value, the more tokens share it.

lensLastBlock.detail: Both numbers come from logits before the checkpoint's generation settings, and the lens takes the last block's row directly from the model's output instead of recomputing it, because a batched recomputation rounds slightly differently. Only the stored rounding can separate the two, so they agree within the tolerance the view states. A larger difference means the stored lens does not belong to this step's output, a recording fault, and the view warns; the generation settings cannot explain it, since neither number includes them. Agreement checks the readout itself; it says nothing about how well the earlier blocks' readouts describe the model.
lensLastBlock.math:
$$\Delta = \big|\lambda^{(B-1)} - \lambda^{\mathrm{out}}\big|, \qquad \lambda^{\mathrm{out}} = \ln \mathrm{softmax}\big(\ell^{(s)}\big)_x$$

- $\lambda^{(B-1)}$: the chosen token's log-probability from the last block's lens; $\lambda^{\mathrm{out}}$: the same from the step's raw output logits $\ell^{(s)}$.
- $\ell^{(s)} = W_U\,\mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(h^{(B-1)}_t)$; the lens takes $\ell^{(s)}$ itself for the last block, so $\Delta$ is only the stored rounding.
- The view warns when $\Delta$ exceeds the stated tolerance.
lensLastBlock.overview: At the last block the lens is the model's real output: its row is taken from the step's raw output logits, not recomputed. The view shows both numbers for the chosen token: its probability from the last block's lens and from the raw model output.

lensNotRecorded.detail: The lens cannot be rebuilt from a finished trace: it needs the full output vector of every block at every step, and a trace without it keeps only residual-norm statistics of the traced blocks and the output candidates. Runs saved before lens recording existed never have it, and a checkpoint with more blocks than the limit traces as before, without a lens. When a run reached its lens size limit, the first steps keep their readouts and later steps say "not kept"; the generated tokens are not affected.
lensNotRecorded.math:
$$p^{(b)}_t = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W_U\, \mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(h^{(b)}_t)\big), \qquad h^{(b)}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$$

- Needs all $d$ components of $h^{(b)}_t$ for every block $b$ and step; $d$ is the checkpoint's hidden size.
- A norm $\lVert h^{(b)}_t \rVert$ or a few top dimensions do not determine $\mathrm{RMSNorm}_f(h^{(b)}_t)$, so the readout cannot be derived from them.
lensNotRecorded.overview: This run has no logit lens. Traces record it only from the node version that added it, and only for checkpoints within the lens block limit.

linearNoMatrix.detail: Instead of a growing KV cache, each value head carries one state matrix of fixed size from token to token. Each token first fades the state, then writes into it, and the output reads the state with the query. Earlier tokens are blended into that matrix and cannot be separated again, so no weight per position exists, measured or otherwise. A full-attention block shows a row where the run recorded one.
linearNoMatrix.math:
$$S_t = \gamma_t S_{t-1} + \beta_t\, \hat k_t \big(v_t - \gamma_t S_{t-1}^{\top} \hat k_t\big)^{\top}, \qquad o_t = S_t^{\top} \hat q_t / \sqrt{d_k}$$

- $S_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d_v}$: state of one value head, the same size at every position.
- $\gamma_t \in (0,1)$: decay; $\beta_t \in (0,1)$: write strength.
- $\hat q_t$, $\hat k_t$: L2-normed query and key; $v_t$: value.

$o_t$ depends on earlier tokens only through $S_{t-1}$, so there is no $a_{t,s}$ to record. The operation `delta` explains the update step by step.
linearNoMatrix.overview: This block uses linear attention (gated delta rule). It never compares the query with each earlier position, so there is no row of weights to show.

notRecorded.detail: The weights cannot be rebuilt from a finished trace: they need the query and the keys of every position, and a trace keeps neither, only residual norms and candidates. Runs saved before attention recording existed never have them. For a new run, turn on "Record attention" in the trace form; it costs storage and some generation time, so leave it off when norms and candidates are enough. Linear-attention blocks have no weights to record in any run.
notRecorded.math:
$$a_{t,s} = \mathrm{softmax}_s\big(\tilde q_t \cdot \tilde k_s / \sqrt{d_h}\big)$$

- Needs $\tilde q_t$ and every $\tilde k_s$, $s \le t$, of the block; a trace without recording stores neither.
- A residual norm $\lVert h_t \rVert$ does not determine $\tilde q_t$ or $\tilde k_s$, so the weights cannot be derived from it.
notRecorded.overview: This run has no attention weights for this block. They are recorded only when a trace starts with "Record attention" on, and then only for the full-attention blocks the node records by default.

routing.detail: Each block's router scores all of its experts at the position the step reads (the last prompt token for the first step, otherwise the token generated before it), keeps the top k and gives them weights. The run records exactly these k expert ids and the weights the experts received, for every block with a router, read by a hook on the router as the model ran. Expert numbers are positions in the block, not names: expert 12 of one block has nothing to do with expert 12 of another. The run used the Hugging Face checkpoint in PyTorch (bf16); the GGUF that "Next token" runs may choose other experts.
routing.math:
$$p^{(b)} = \mathrm{softmax}\big(W^{(b)}_r\, x'^{(b)}_t\big), \qquad S^{(b)}_s = \mathrm{TopK}_k\big(p^{(b)}\big)$$

- $t = P+s-1$: the position step $s$ reads; $b$: a block with a router.
- $x'^{(b)}_t$: the normed input of block $b$'s feed-forward part at $t$; $W^{(b)}_r$: its router.
- Recorded per step and block: the ids in $S^{(b)}_s$ and their weights $w^{(b)}_e$.

Only the position the step reads is recorded; during the prefill the router also ran on every other prompt position.
routing.overview: For the chosen step, this shows which experts each mixture-of-experts block sent the token through, and with which weights. It is the routing used to predict this token, read from each block's router while the model ran.

routingCaveats.detail: Three limits apply. An expert is not a topic or a skill: routers are trained to spread tokens over the experts, and what an expert adds depends on its weights and on the rest of the block, so a label such as "the math expert" cannot be read off these ids. One prompt is not specialization: the picks of one run reflect this prompt and its answer; a claim about what an expert handles needs many prompts and a controlled comparison, which this view does not make. And this is the Hugging Face checkpoint in PyTorch, not the GGUF that "Next token" runs: quantization changes the router's logits slightly, so where two experts score almost the same the GGUF can pick the other one, and its tokens can then differ too.
routingCaveats.math:
$$S = \mathrm{TopK}_k\big(\mathrm{softmax}(W_r\,x')\big)$$

- $p_{(k)}$, $p_{(k+1)}$: the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-th largest router probabilities.
- A small change in $W_r$ or $x'$ (quantization, another kernel) changes $S$ when it moves these two past each other, which takes little when $p_{(k)} - p_{(k+1)}$ is small.
- The ids in $S$ are positions in the block's expert tensors; nothing in the model attaches a meaning to them.
routingCaveats.overview: Routing shows which experts ran, not what they mean. An expert is not a topic, one prompt does not show specialization, and the GGUF may route differently.

routingNotRecorded.detail: Routing cannot be rebuilt from a finished trace: it needs each block's router output at every step, and a trace without it keeps only residual-norm statistics and output candidates. Runs saved before routing recording existed never have it, a dense checkpoint has no router to read, and steering runs do not record it. When a run reached its routing size limit, the first steps keep their rows and later steps say "not kept"; the generated tokens are not affected.
routingNotRecorded.math:
$$S^{(b)}_s = \mathrm{TopK}_k\big(\mathrm{softmax}(W^{(b)}_r\, x'^{(b)}_{P+s-1})\big)$$

- Needs all $d$ components of $x'^{(b)}_{P+s-1}$, the normed input of block $b$'s feed-forward part, at every step; a residual norm or a few top dimensions do not determine it.
- A dense block has no $W_r$, so there is nothing to record.
routingNotRecorded.overview: This run has no routing. Traces record it only from the node version that added it, and only for checkpoints whose blocks have a mixture-of-experts router.

routingUsage.detail: For the selected block, every recorded step counts one pick for each expert it chose; the list shows the experts picked most often and in how many steps. When the run reached its routing size limit, only the saved steps count, and the view says how many. The counts describe this one prompt and its answer: an expert picked in many steps here is not shown to handle a topic, and another prompt can spread the picks quite differently.
routingUsage.math:
$$c_e = \big|\{\, s \in R : e \in S^{(b)}_s \,\}\big|, \qquad \sum_e c_e = k\,|R|$$

- $R$: the recorded steps (every generated token, or the saved ones when the run was cut at its size limit).
- $S^{(b)}_s$: the experts block $b$ chose at step $s$; $c_e$: in how many of those steps expert $e$ was picked.
- If the router spread its picks evenly, each expert would be picked in about $k\,|R| / n_{\text{exp}}$ steps.
routingUsage.overview: Counts how often each expert of the selected block was chosen over the steps of this run. It is derived from the recorded routing, not something the model computed.

routingWeights.detail: The weights are the ones the experts actually received: the router probabilities of the chosen experts in bf16, stored bit for bit; the chips round them for display only. Some models divide them by their sum so they add up to 1 (the run states whether this checkpoint does); others keep the raw probabilities, which then add up to less than 1. The view then also shows their sum: the share of the router's probability that fell on the chosen experts; a small share means the router spread its probability over many experts. A large weight means that expert's output counts more in this block's mix, not that the expert matters more for the token: the mix is then added to the residual stream like every other block's output.
routingWeights.math:
$$w_e = p_e \;\; (\text{not renormalized}), \qquad w_e = \frac{p_e}{\sum_{j \in S} p_j} \;\; (\text{renormalized}), \qquad e \in S$$

$$y = \sum_{e \in S} w_e\, E_e(x')$$

- $p_e$: router probability of expert $e$; $S$: the chosen experts; $E_e$: expert $e$'s output.
- Shown sum, only when not renormalized: $\sum_{e \in S} w_e \le 1$, the share of the probability on the chosen experts.
- Stored: the 16 bits of each bf16 weight, so the view reads exactly the value the expert's output was multiplied by.
routingWeights.overview: Each chosen expert's weight says how strongly its output counts in the block's mix. The chips show the weights rounded; the stored values are exact.

step.detail: The prompt pass (prefill) runs every prompt token through all blocks; the output at its last position gives the candidates for the first generated token. Each later step reads one token: full-attention blocks look up the keys and values of all earlier positions in the KV cache, which grows by one entry per step, and linear-attention blocks update their fixed-size state. The trace decodes greedily, so the chosen token is the top candidate after the checkpoint's generation settings. Everything shown comes from this one saved run of the Hugging Face checkpoint in bf16, not from the GGUF that "Next token" runs.
step.math:
$$\ell^{(s)} = f\big(x_0, \dots, x_{P+s-1}\big)_{P+s-1}, \qquad x_{P+s} = \arg\max_i \tilde\ell^{(s)}_i$$

- $P$: number of prompt tokens; positions count from 0.
- $s$: index of the generated token, from 0. Its step reads position $P+s-1$: the last prompt token for $s = 0$, otherwise generated token $s-1$.
- $\ell^{(s)}$: logits at that position; $\tilde\ell^{(s)}$: the same after the checkpoint's processors.

With the cache, a step computes only its own position in each block and reads the $P+s$ cached keys of each full-attention block; the prefill computes all prompt positions in one pass, with the same result up to rounding.
step.overview: One step of the replay is one forward pass of the model that produces one generated token. The first step reads the whole prompt at once; every later step feeds in only the token chosen before it.

topKeys.detail: The run sets K and states it; a row shorter than K keeps every key. Each kept weight is rounded down to a multiple of 1/10,000, so a weight below 0.01 % shows as 0 and the shown values never exceed the true ones. The rest is the combined weight of all keys that were not kept, one number per row and head; which positions it falls on is not stored. A small rest means the kept keys cover almost the whole row; a large rest means the head spreads its weight thinly. Because of the rounding, kept weights and rest can add up to slightly less than 100 %. The list shows the kept keys in position order, with one neighbour on each side for context.
topKeys.math:
$$\mathcal{K}_t = \text{positions of the } \min(K,\, t+1) \text{ largest } a_{t,s}, \quad s \le t$$

$$\hat a_{t,s} = \frac{\lfloor 10^4\, a_{t,s} \rfloor}{10^4} \;\; (s \in \mathcal{K}_t), \qquad r_t = 1 - \sum_{s \in \mathcal{K}_t} a_{t,s}$$

- $t$: query position; the row has $t+1$ keys.
- $\hat a$: stored weight; $r_t$: the rest.

$\sum_{s \in \mathcal{K}_t} \hat a_{t,s} + r_t \le 1$. The kernel does not return weights; they are computed beside it in fp32 from the same post-RoPE query and keys, for every head of the block.
topKeys.overview: A row over a long prompt has thousands of weights. The run keeps only the K largest per row and head, plus one number for all others: the rest.

maxP99.detail: For each step the tracer computes the 1st, 50th and 99th percentile over the dimensions of the block output at the newest position, on signed values. The summary keeps the largest 99th percentile over all steps. One step is enough to set it, and it says nothing about large negative values.
maxP99.math:
$$P = \max_s Q_{0.99}\big(h_{s,1}, \dots, h_{s,d}\big)$$

- $s$: recorded steps with a finite 99th percentile.
- $h_{s,i}$: dimension $i$ of the block output at the newest position in step $s$.
- $Q_{0.99}$: 99th percentile over the $d$ dimensions, linearly interpolated (`torch.quantile`).
maxP99.overview: The highest 99th percentile of the output values seen at this block. It hints at large positive values among the dimensions.

meanNorm.detail: The trace records one value per forward step: the prompt pass (its last token), then each generated token that is fed back in. Each value is the L2 norm of the block output at the newest position only. The summary averages them. It is measured on the Hugging Face checkpoint and joined to this file by block index. A large norm does not mean the block is important or caused the chosen token.
meanNorm.math:
$$\bar n = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N} \lVert h_s \rVert_2$$

- $h_s$: block output at the newest position in step $s$.
- $N$: recorded steps with a finite norm; a byte cap can end a long trace early.
- $\lVert h \rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_i h_i^2}$.
meanNorm.overview: The average length of this block's output vector over the traced steps. It shows how large the residual stream is at this depth, nothing more.

topDimensions.detail: Per step the tracer records the 8 dimensions with the largest absolute value at the newest position. The summary counts how often each index appears over all steps and lists the 5 most frequent, lower index first on ties. Such recurring large dimensions are common in language models. They do not explain why a token was chosen, and a link to the output is correlation, not cause.
topDimensions.math:
$$T_s = \operatorname{top}_8\big(|h_{s,i}|\big), \qquad c_i = \sum_s [\,i \in T_s\,]$$

The summary lists the 5 indices with the highest $c_i$.

- $T_s$: the 8 indices with the largest $|h_{s,i}|$ in step $s$.
- $c_i$: number of steps with index $i$ in their top 8.
- $[\cdot]$: 1 when true, else 0.
topDimensions.overview: The dimensions that most often had one of the largest absolute values at this block. A dimension that keeps appearing carries unusually large values; that is not the same as being important.
